Prepare the Pan: • Line a 9x13-inch baking dish with parchment paper. 2. Melt Butter and Marshmallows: • In a large saucepan over low heat, melt the butter. • Add the mini marshmallows and stir continuously until completely melted and smooth. • Stir in the Irish cream syrup and salt (if using). 3. Combine with Rice Cereal: • Quickly fold in the rice cereal, making sure every piece is evenly coated with the marshmallow mixture. • Gently stir in the Lucky Charm marshmallows. If desired, add a few drops of green food coloring for extra festivity. 4. Transfer and Set: • Immediately press the mixture evenly into the prepared baking dish. • Press extra Lucky Charm marshmallows on top for decoration or sprinkle with edible glitter for a festive touch. 5. Cool and Serve: • Let the treats cool at room temperature for about 30 minutes before cutting into squares. We were in London but moved there for more green space. It’s close enough to London, not too far away.The Prince and Princess of Wales moved into the home earlier this month, as their kids, Prince George, 12, Princess Charlotte, 10, and Prince Louis, 7, were on their school break. The family previously lived at Adelaide Cottage since 2022. The properties are both located inside Windsor Great Park, and are about four miles apart.Kate and William’s new 328-year-old Georgian mansion is larger than their old place—about twice the size—and more fitting for their future, as their kids are quickly growing into teens. It has eight bedrooms, and its amenities include a ballroom and a tennis court. content: This is your PSA to make a batch of beef stew and bake it with a puff pastry topper. You’re welcome This is cold weather comfort food and when you happen to decorate it with some puff pastry shamrocks ☘️☘️, we can also call it St. Patrick’s Day food! . . Beef Pot Pie with Puff Pastry Crust . . *also, for this batch, I didn’t add potatoes, but substituted mushrooms instead. It’s a completely forgiving recipe. Use what you have to make it your own 2-3 lbs stew meat patted dry and seasoned with salt & pepper. I used boneless beef chuck-eye roast cut into 1” pieces. 1/3 cup flour 1/4 cup oil 1 onion chopped 3 carrots, peeled and cut into 1” pieces 4 garlic cloves chopped 1/3 cup tomato paste 1 cup red wine 4 cups beef broth 2 tbls soy sauce 3 tbls Worcestershire sauce 1 bay leaf 5 sprigs of fresh thyme 2 cups tiny new potatoes 1 cup frozen peas 1/3 cup fresh chopped parsley Egg wash (1 beaten egg mixed with 1 tbls water) 1 sheet puffed pastry Heat oven to 350F. Toss beef with flour to coat. Heat oil in a Dutch oven & sear beef in batches. Put in a bowl and set aside. To the drippings add onion, garlic and carrots and cook until vegetables are softened. Stir in tomato paste and cook 5 minutes stirring constantly. Stir in wine (or water) and cook until evaporated scraping the bottom of pot.. Add broth, soy sauce, Worcestershire, bay leaf and thyme. Scraping up any bits. Add beef and bring to a simmer. Cover and transfer to oven. Cook until beef is tender, about 1 1/2 hours. Remove filling from oven and add potatoes. Bake 30 minutes more. Remove bay and thyme sprigs. Add peas and parsley and check for seasoning. Let cool 20 minutes. Add beef mixture to a cast iron skillet or a casserole dish. Brush the rim with eggwash. Roll pastry sheet out to slightly overlap dish and lay over casserole trimming corners if necessary. Cut a cross in the center of pie and brush with egg wash. Transfer to a baking sheet lined with parchment and bake until crust is golden brown, 20-30 minutes. . . . . #beefstewrecipe #beefpotpie #puffpastryrecipes #cozyfood #beefstew

I appreciate all of your encouragement and support. #stparicksday #vodka #sourapple #caramel #apples #applenachos #cocktails #appletini Green Apple Nachos You can serve them as a snack for kids or a festive treat for adults, these green apple nachos are sure to be a hit at your St. Patrick’s Day celebration! Number of Servings: 4 servings Ingredients: * 2 large green apples (such as Granny Smith), sliced * ½ cup caramel sauce * ½ cup chocolate sauce * ¼ cup chopped nuts (such as walnuts or pecans) * ¼ cup mini marshmallows (optional) * Green sprinkles (for decoration, optional) Instructions: 1. Arrange the sliced green apples on a large serving platter or plate. 2. Drizzle caramel sauce over the apple slices. 3. Drizzle the chocolate sauce over the apples as well. 4. Sprinkle chopped nuts and mini marshmallows over the top. 5. Add green sprinkles for a festive touch, if desired. 6. Serve immediately and enjoy! Sour Appletini Cocktail Ingredients: 1 oz Vodka (I’m using Tito's) 3 oz Finest Call Sour Apple Martini Mix 1 oz Rose's Sweetened Lime Juice (optional) Instructions: Combine ingredients in an ice filled shaker. content: On St. Patrick's day, you probably could have guessed that it would come down to Glenn McCarthy. Glenn led one of the wildest Texas lives of all time and his rags to riches to (almost) rags story is Shakespearean and should be the subject of a Netflix miniseries. Glenn was proud of his Irish roots, exceedingly so, so much that when he opened his hotel in Houston he called it the Shamrock and had 2500 shamrocks flown in from Ireland. The Shamrock was a $21-million extravaganza that Glenn built from 1946-1949. The grand opening of the hotel was (naturally) on St. Patrick’s Day, 1949, with a party that cost more than one million dollars. Hollywood stars arrived by plane and by train and 5,000 guests reveled in its 63 shades of green decor. Billed as “Houston’s biggest party,” it cemented his reputation as the quintessential Texas oilman—brash, flamboyant, and larger-than-life. The Shamrock symbolized his vision for Houston as a modern powerhouse. The Shamrock soon faced ongoing struggles with occupancy rates and was rarely, if ever, fully booked. McCarthy had spent extravagantly and then borrowed heavily against his assets, including the hotel, to fund a series of risky investments. His cash reserves quickly dwindled, and within a year, manager George Lindholm quietly resigned. In 1952, after defaulting on a loan, McCarthy lost the hotel to the Equitable Life Assurance Society. That same year, author Edna Ferber immortalized the Shamrock as the "Conquistador" in her novel Giant, and it later made a brief appearance in the 1956 film adaptation directed by George Stevens. Despite its financial woes, the Shamrock thrived as a social hub during the early 1950s. With its restaurants, bars, and upscale shops, it earned the nickname "Houston’s Riviera." The hotel’s exclusive Cork Club became a hotspot for oil deals (and reportedly, the occasional fistfight), while also hosting performances by Frank Sinatra. In 1953, Patty Andrews of the Andrews Sisters launched her short-lived solo career in the hotel’s stylish Emerald Room nightclub. In 1954, Hilton Hotels Corporation took over management of the Shamrock and purchased it in 1955 at a price well below its original construction cost. However, Hilton also struggled to make the massive hotel profitable. Its location, removed from downtown Houston and the city’s expanding freeway system, put it at a disadvantage. The Shamrock faced increasing competition from smaller, cheaper, and more car-friendly motels. In 1957, a low two-story “lanai” wing was added near the swimming pool to provide motel-style accommodations. Meanwhile, the anticipated shopping and entertainment district never materialized, as affluent homebuyers opted for other parts of Houston. However, McCarthy’s vision later influenced the development of the Houston Galleria, which opened in 1970 at a prime freeway intersection on the city’s west side. Around 1965, Texas’s first Trader Vic’s restaurant opened in the Shamrock and remained in business until after 1985. The hotel continued hosting social events such as debutante balls, barbecues, and business gatherings, operating as the Shamrock Hilton until 1986—by which time its prestige had long faded. During the oil bust in 1986, the 36-year-old hotel, still the second largest in Houston but by then in need of extensive refurbishing and refitting, was in effect donated to the Texas Medical Center. In March 1986 a protest rally was held by historic preservationists including McCarthy, and the hotel opened its last annual St. Patrick's Day party to the public. That evening, some people who had been at the opening night party in 1949 reportedly attended a semi-formal event in the hotel's Emerald Room. A few employees had been with the hotel since its first year of operation. The main hotel building was demolished on June 1, 1987 and the land was paved over as a surface parking lot. Glenn McCarthy died 18 months later at the age of 81. He was living in a modest house in La Porte at the time of his death. Shown here: the Shamrock Hotel at the time of its grand opening in 1949.

title: GREEN FOOD | @elliotts.kitchen
content: Here’s some Green Food to celebrate St. Patrick’s Day with your family. Kind of a lot of pesto but whatever.. we like pesto. We got: Shrimp Pesto Pasta Green Goddess Steak Salad Pesto Prosciutto Grilled Pizza Avocado Feta Dip #stpatricksday #green #dinnerideas Shrimp Pesto Pasta Ingredients: Asparagus 1 lb shrimp, deveined and peeled 1 lb pasta 1/2 cup pine nuts 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice 1 garlic clove Salt Pepper 2 cups basil leaves 1/4 cup extra virgin olive oil 1/4 cup parmigiano reggiano Instructions: 1. Cut asparagus into 2 inch pieces and add to a medium heat pan. 2. Season with olive oil, salt, pepper, garlic powder and cook for ~5 minutes until done. Remove from heat and set aside. 3. Prep shrimp by patting dry and season with salt and pepper. 4. Add to thee same pan on medium high heat. Cook for about 2 minutes on one side and 1 minute on the second side until a nice pink color. 5. Add pasta to boiling water. 6. In a foodprocessor, combine pine nuts, lemon juice, garlic, salt and pepper and pulse. 7. Add the basil and pulse again. 8. With the food processor running, drizzle the olive oil and pulse til combined. 9. Add parmesan cheese and pulse again. Add more olive oil if you want it smoother. 10. Set aside 1/4 cup of pasta water. 11. In the pot add shrimp, asparagus and cooked pasta. Add a spoonful of pesto and pasta water. Stir to combine. Add more pesto and pasta water as needed (the pasta water will make it creamier). 12. Serve and enjoy! Green Goddess Steak Salad Ingredients: 1/2 cup mayo 1 cup greek yogurt 1 oz fresh basil leaves, finely chopped 2 tbsp shallot, minced 2 tbsp basil pesto 1/4 cup white wine vinegar 1 tbsp + 1 tsp agave syrup (we subbed for maple syrup) 1 tsp dijon mustard Salt pepper Salad Composition: Romaine Green Goddess Dressing Cherry Tomatoes Red Onion Avocado Steak More Dressing Instructions: 1. Add all dressing ingredients in a mason jar and blend together. Refrigerate while you prepare the rest of your salad. 2. Prep your veggies: romaine. cherry tomatoes, red onion, avocado. 3. Salt steak and grill til desired temperature. Let rest and slice. 4. Build your salad, serve and enjoy! Pesto Prosciutto Grilled Pizza Ingredients: Pizza Dough Pesto Mozzarella Prosciutto Avocado oil Salt Pepper Instructions: 1. Place the pizza stone and pizza insert bottom grate of the Masterbuilt. 2. Add charcoal and light it. Set temperature to 525F. 3. Prep dough by sprinkling AP flour and rolling/stretching out dough to a circle (we use homemade dough from our grocery store). 4. Sprinkle semolina flour onto pizza peel and put your dough on top to decorate. We did pesto base, mozzarella, and prosciutto on top. 5. Brush EVOO on the crust and head to your grill. 6. Check if the grill is not TOO hot by throwing semolina flour onto the pizza stone. If it lights on fire the temperature is too high. 7. Slide pizza in and close the grill for about 3-4 minutes or until the crust starts to get brown on top. 8. Use the peel to rotate the pizza every few minutes to make sure it’s not sticking. 9. Slice it up, serve and enjoy! Avocado Feta Dip Ingredients: 4 tbsp fresh dill, chopped 4 tbsp chives, chopped 2 tbsp fresh mint, chopped 2 ripe avocados 2 cups Greek yogurt 1/4 cup lemon juice, fresh squeezed Salt 1/2 lb feta, diced Instructions: 1. Prep herbs and add to a food processor or small blender with avocado, greek yogurt, lemon juice and salt. 2. Pulse or just blend to mix altogether then add feta and pulse/blend again. 3. Serve immediately with your choice of chips or veggies. Enjoy!

title: Witches "Hating" on Saint Patrick's Day? Try THIS.
content: Every year, I see the meme go around on Saint Patrick's Day, where the pagans remind the world that the snakes in the story ARE the pagans. And there has been some debate on the historical accuracy of all of it. This is what I do with that energy in the NOW. Once upon a time, I picked up the idea from another witchy pagan that the thing to do with these celebration days is to gather up all that energy and actually use it for something. I'm talking in the witchy sense - energetically or magickally gather it up. I usually do this work in silence, as I've put it to action in churches, and parties, or other times where folks come together to celebrate. (Usually, it's in silence. Me chatting about it today ISN'T silence, in wanting to share the concept with other witches out there. ) The idea is that they are creating or raising all of this energy, and not doing ANYTHING with it. So, why shouldn't I? This year, I went into the St. Patrick's day celebrations with intentions. The first intention was to have a good time, but also my friend and I had been working on a specific manifestation. It was serious, and we were too seriously focused I think, in hindsight. When we arrived, I took joy in the decorated tables, all the green shamrocks and wigs and how everyone was in something green. It was a delight. Then we saw the prize table for a raffle draw that was to take place. We focused on our delight in seeing a cedar raised garden bed as one of the prizes, and playfully made "conjuring hands" over the prize. I delighted in taking extra cash out of the ATM in the legion, and even made sure that my energy when spending an entire $20 on tickets was made in the energy of play and love. And hot damn, we won that prize. There were about 80 prizes to be won on the tables, and a LOT of tickets sold. We were the 4th and 5th in line. Tickets went on sale at 2pm. We won the prize by 2:07. Our second very serious manifestation intention didn't happen that day. I think we may have been TOO intense about that topic. But because we were light and playful and easy with the cedar garden bed, that came easy. All this to say, pay attention to how you can use love today on the Saint Patrick's Day celebrations going on around you, even if you don't like the story. Begin with a classic green and white color palette, incorporating soft, muted greens alongside crisp whites and subtle gold accents. Elevate your space with floral arrangements featuring lilies, daffodils, and ivy, placed in vintage vases or rustic pitchers. Wooden accents, such as antique furniture or handcrafted trays, add warmth and depth, while garlands of ivy or eucalyptus draped over mantles and staircases bring a natural, festive touch. Thoughtfully curated Irish symbols, like Celtic knot throw pillows or shamrock-themed artwork, provide a sophisticated nod to the holiday without overwhelming the space. Set a refined St. Patrick’s Day table with vintage china, linen tablecloths, and gold flatware, creating an inviting space for guests. Soft textures, such as green velvet cushions and wool throws, enhance the cozy ambiance, while candles and lanterns add a warm glow. Framed botanical prints, antique mirrors, and vintage Irish ceramics serve as elegant decorative elements throughout the home. Enhance the entryway with a welcoming wreath and subtle Irish-themed accents, setting the tone for a stylish celebration. A cozy seating area, accented with green patterns and plush fabrics, ensures comfort while maintaining a polished look. Complete the celebration with a beautifully arranged drink and treat display featuring Irish coffee, whiskey, or festive green punch served in fine glassware. Arrange traditional Irish sweets on vintage serving trays, surrounded by candlelight and greenery for an elevated touch. This is the reason that I have completely turned away from Dior's Quints since their disastrous reformulations. Both of these Quints just look as if they've been bleached under the Australian Sun. It's certainly not what I think of when it comes to Spring. Dior should be ashamed of themselves for putting out such underwhelming performing products at this price. All of this talk about the lip products changing to suit the Ph. As for the decorations on the end of the lipsticks, I thought that what was said to be a number eight could in fact be the infinity symbol (?). content: You have reduced culture to decoration, food, and festivals. That is not what people mean when they say they are worried about replacement. We are talking about an operating system, the average traits of a people writ large. A dominant common language. High trust with strangers. Low corruption. Rule following. Impersonal institutions over kin networks. A shared national story thick enough that people accept losses, obey outcomes, and feel obligations to people they will never meet. You dodge the only questions that matter about immigrant. Who. From where. How many. Scale, rate, assimilation. At high volumes, with no assimilation pressure, “America can include everything” stops meaning newcomers join a mainstream and starts meaning parallel publics, bilingual mass culture, bloc politics, and managed fragmentation. Your post is a love letter to that outcome, dressed up as tolerance and status signalling. “Democracy, freedom, Constitution” is downstream of a specific culture. They only work when the population has the norms to sustain them. Import large numbers from low trust, high kinship societies and pretend a civic creed will do the work, and you are not defending America. You are describing how it rots from the inside. So no, people are not too narrow. You are too superficial. You think an immigrant is a food truck and a flag. You cannot even name the deep thing you insist cannot be replaced. QT @HistoryBoomer: "Immigrants are going to replace our culture!" What culture is that, exactly? Is it the Iowa State Fair? Seeing the Hawkeyes play the Cyclones on Saturday night? Eating pork chops on a stick? Church choirs volunteering to help rebuild homes after a tornado? Is it barbacoa on Sunday morning before mass and your little girl's quinceañera? Or accordion-driven Tejano music playing from a pickup truck? Is it moms dropping their kids off for Calabasas ballet in Range Rovers and Teslas? Lululemon and Vuori? Angry meetings about fence heights at the HOA? Is it salsa coming through open windows on hot days? Folding chairs gathered around a domino game? Puerto Rican and American flags everywhere to honor Marines coming home? Is it Southern comfort food at Mary Mac's Tea Room? Morehouse and Spelman grads meeting to network? Southern rap blasting at Magic City? People afraid of being "replaced" have too narrow a view of what America is about. And yes, America can include a statue of the Hindu god Hanuman in Houston. (Because, c'mon, what is more over-the-top Texan than a 90-foot golden statue of a dude wielding a huge bad-ass club?) My American culture doesn't discriminate based on ethnic background. My American culture is one that can deal with immigrants because it embraces their myriad varieties. My American culture holds dear democracy, freedom, and independence. My America believes in self-governance, from jury rooms, where 12 strangers gather to decide a fellow citizen's fate, to town halls, to local elections, to national campaigns. It's watching locals grill an annoyed city council about a new park or too much crime downtown. My America believes in free speech so much that we put it at the top of the Bill of Rights. I get to call my leaders idiots and feel no fear of prison or punishment. I believe in allowing marches and protests, from the good ones (Selma and Stonewall) to the ones I dislike (Proud Boys or Antifa). My America is proud to see rows of new citizens lined up at city hall, with many different skin tones but the same expression of hope and anticipation. Because my America is Ronald Reagan's America, "still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home." So it's ok if some people march in a St Patrick's Day parade while others celebrate the Vietnamese (Tet) New Year, as long as they are all committed to freedom, democracy, the Constitution, and this amazing thing called "America." 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

content: ☘️Gluten-Free Green Velvet Cupcakes☘️ These are the perfect treat to make this coming St. Patrick’s Day! Here’s how to make them: 🧁Ingredients🧁 1 1⁄4 cups gluten free flour blend 1 teaspoon baking powder 1⁄2 teaspoon plus 1⁄4 teaspoon kosher or fine sea salt, divided 1⁄4 teaspoon baking soda 1 cup unsalted butter, at room temperature, divided 3⁄4 cup granulated sugar 2 large eggs, at room temperature 1 tablespoon plus 1 teaspoon Singing Dog Vanilla Organic Vanilla Extract, divided 1⁄2 cup buttermilk Green gel food coloring 8 ounces cream cheese, at room temperature 4 cups powdered sugar Sprinkles 🧁Recipe🧁 Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a standard muffin tin with cupcake liners. In a mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, 1⁄2 teaspoon salt, and baking soda. In the bowl of an electric mixer, preferably fitted with the paddle attachment, beat 1⁄2 cup butter with the sugar on medium-high speed for 5 minutes. Scape down the sides of the bowl as needed. Add the eggs, one at a time, beating well and scraping down the sides of the bowl after each addition. Beat in 1 tablespoon vanilla. Scrape down the sides of the bowl. Turn down the mixer to medium, add 1/3 of the flour mixture, then half the buttermilk, another third of the flour mixture, the rest of the buttermilk, and finally, the rest of the flour. Add enough food coloring to get a vibrant green. Give the batter a final mix by hand with a spatula. Divide the batter evenly among the prepared muffin tins (an ice cream scoop works well for this). Bake for 18–20 minutes or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. Let cool in the pan for 10 minutes then remove to a wire rack to finish cooling. For the frosting, cream together the remining 1⁄2 cup butter, 1⁄4 teaspoon salt, and cream cheese. Beat on medium-high speed until creamy. Beat in 1 teaspoon vanilla. Turn the mixer to low and gradually add the powdered sugar. Beat until completely combined. Frost the cooled cupcakes generously and decorate with sprinkles. content: 17 DE MARZO SAN PATRICIO "Yo era como una piedra en una profunda mina; y aquel que es poderoso vino, y en su misericordia, me levantó y me puso sobre una pared”, escribió alguna vez San Patricio, Patrono de Irlanda, cuya fiesta se celebra cada 17 de marzo. San Patricio nació en Britania (Gran Bretaña) alrededor del año 385. Siendo joven fue llevado cautivo a la isla de Irlanda. Allí trabajó como esclavo durante seis años. Cuando recobró la libertad, siguió el camino del sacerdocio y, en la madurez, llegó a ser Obispo de aquella tierra. El patronazgo de Irlanda lo ostenta junto a Santa Brígida y San Columba. San Patricio es considerado por la tradición como el que introdujo el cristianismo en Irlanda ya que se convirtió en el más grande misionero de la isla en los tiempos de la expansión del Evangelio en la Europa Insular. Célebre es la historia que da cuenta de la sencillez con la que explicaba realidades tan complejas como la naturaleza divina. San Patricio solía usar una hoja de trébol de tres puntas para explicar la Trinidad, haciendo una analogía entre las tres puntas de la hoja de trébol y las tres personas divinas, distintas y distinguibles pero que componen una sola realidad. En el caso de la Trinidad, Dios Padre, Dios Hijo y Dios Espíritu Santo, pero un solo Dios verdadero. Como obispo, San Patricio se enfrentó a los druidas, paganos que controlaban políticamente el territorio insular, y a los pelagianos, herejes que por ese entonces confundían a los fieles cristianos. San Patricio, en un contexto tan difícil como ese, no cesó en el esfuerzo por lograr la unidad doctrinal de los católicos, mientras extendía el cristianismo y su cultura por Irlanda, construyendo abadías y más templos. Se dice que un Sábado Santo, cuando San Patricio encendió el fuego pascual, un grupo de druidas intentó apagarlo sin tener éxito. Entonces uno de ellos exclamó con pesar: "El fuego de la religión que Patricio ha encendido, se extenderá por toda la isla". Con el tiempo aquella queja se tornó en profecía, porque el cristianismo efectivamente se extendió por toda Irlanda. Una de las mayores preocupaciones del Santo fue la formación de un clero local. Dios bendijo su celo pastoral atrayendo a muchos hombres al sacerdocio. El florecimiento de las vocaciones permitió que la Iglesia se organice mejor, con mayor solidez, a través de la presencia de obispos en todo el territorio. Al final de su vida, San Patricio escribió sus “Confesiones”, obra autobiográfica en la que plasmó sus memorias, tanto las vicisitudes que sufrió al estar al servicio de Dios como su sentir sobre lo que debía ser el crecimiento del Pueblo de Dios en Britania. San Patricio influyó positivamente en la reforma de las leyes civiles de Irlanda a través de principios propios de la moral católica. Entre otras cosas, el reconocimiento de aquel legado es indispensable para valorar la contribución de este santo, como de la Iglesia en general, en la formación de la nación irlandesa y del espíritu británico. San Patricio fue convocado a la Casa del Padre el año 461 y fue sepultado en Saúl, región de Stragford Lough, lugar en donde él mandó edificar su primera iglesia. La devoción por San Patricio se ha extendido por todo el mundo, de manera particular en los países de habla inglesa, gracias a la presencia de la inmigración proveniente de Irlanda. En los lugares donde hay comunidades de irlandeses, se acostumbra celebrar con decoraciones y vestimentas de color verde -el color nacional- y se organizan marchas o desfiles que aglutinan no solo a los devotos sino a personas de todas las razas, credos y culturas, como es el caso de la celebración que se lleva a cabo en la ciudad de Nueva York (Estados Unidos). Allí, por ejemplo, una de las tradiciones más antiguas es el desfile por el día de San Patricio (“St. Patrick's Day), que data desde tiempos coloniales. En sus inicios, el desfile era protagonizado por los irlandeses que formaban parte del ejército británico, quienes solían vestirse de verde y entonaban canciones típicas al son de las gaitas. Ese espíritu ha permanecido en el tiempo y hoy dicho desfile es una de las celebraciones más grandes de la ciudad estadounidense. El color representativo sigue siendo el verde y los participantes -en su mayoría locales- pasan frente a la Catedral de San Patricio.

content: Chicago’s beloved St. Patrick’s Day tradition kicked off earlier today as the city transformed its river into a striking emerald green, signalling the start of a lively weekend of festivities. Thousands of spectators lined the riverfront between State and Columbus, eagerly watching as boats dispersed the environmentally safe dye, turning the water a brilliant shade of green. The spectacle, a cherished annual event, lasted for around five hours, drawing both locals and visitors alike. The celebrations continue with the highly anticipated Chicago St. Patrick’s Day Parade, set to begin at 12:30 p.m. The parade will feature an array of Irish dancers, marching bands, and elaborately decorated floats, creating a vibrant display of Irish heritage and community spirit.
